meta.title: Amazon kept shutting down my tablet, so I spent $266 on four AI models to own it
meta.author: Yogthos

comments.author: JulianSildenLanglo
comments.text: I wish people had a right to root-access on pretty much every device they own. Manufacturers shouldn't be allowed to deny it.

comments.author: justJanne
comments.text:
To actually be able to use this right, you'll also have to ban services from requiring hardware attestation. If the user wants hardware attestation, great, but if they don't, they should still be able to access everything they want.

Look at the Android ROM scene for example, which was relatively healthy, until many apps started to require attestation, which means even users who could become root or install custom ROMs can't do so on their daily driver devices.

comments.author: lake
comments.text:
Yeah. GrapheneOS fares here better than most other Android ROMs because in the standard installation it runs with a re-locked bootloader, and doesn't allow root access. With those, it passes the basic Play Integrity checks, but does fail the strict Play Integrity ones (the ones that require your OS to be what your OEM shipped ... even if it's years out of date). Fortunately, none of my regular apps still require those, but it's a problem for some, especially afaik with government apps in the EU.

But yeah, it's otherwise pretty bad, and even Graphene has to put in a lot of work to retain compatibility.

comments.author: valenterry
comments.text:
No. You can also re-lock the bootloader with other ROMs.

The reason GrapheneOS apparently fares better is because companies are approving their keys/signature. Which also means you now cannot modify GrapheneOS even if it's open source.

It's pretty terrible and it's long overdue that such practices are being strictly regulated (i.e. forbidden) by the states.

comments.author: BenjaminRi
comments.text:
To actually be able to use this right, you'll also have to ban services from requiring hardware attestation


Good, let's do that. It's overdue for about a decade.

comments.author: mdaniel
comments.text:
As a bit of hair splitting, the right != the obligation, so (take this specific example) a user can decide they no longer need to do banking apps on their dashboard device in the kitchen and opt-in to unlocking their hardware to do with as they see fit

And, if I correctly understand the ecosystem, that is not a one-way door - so if they wanted to try out a new fancy ROM, and then decide they prefer being back on vanilla, such a right would enable putting it back onto the "supported" distribution and be back on the happy path from the perspective of those banking gatekeepers.

comments.author: JulianSildenLanglo
comments.text: I'd frankly even be ok with it popping a fuse in the chip as long as it made it very clear that that would happen.

comments.author: lake
comments.text: I agree. The fact that the majority of mobile phones and tablet manufacturers are somewhere on the "just terrible" and "avoid at all costs" sections of the bootloader unlock wall of shame (Apple and Samsung being the biggest ones) is just ... terrible. Apple of course originally set the lead by showing that you can dominate the market with completely locked down devices, but the fact that most of the industry has followed has been one of the biggest setbacks for open computing and the right to do what you want with your hardware.

comments.author: simonw
comments.text:

comments.author: strugee
comments.text: I had success (a while ago) in just telling Claude to find a novel exploit. It doesn't take much to push it off doing research on existing work.

comments.author: altano
comments.text:
This article is a good case study in how hard it is to erase AI-voice. It’s almost there, so close, and yet what remains is awful and annoying.

It seems hard to start with a foundation of AI prose and end up with something good, even if your intention is to heavily rewrite.

comments.author: DustyFuzzy
comments.text:
I know from having to do it constantly with what my coworkers spit out, that the only way to do it is to have it on the side as reference material, and write everything from scratch instead.

The benefit is that whoever does the prompting can request the AI to be more verbose, and leave separating the wheat from the chaff to a human, who tend to do a better job at it. Models still have a habit of getting stuck on some small irrelevant detail.

comments.author: altano
comments.text: Yeah, having it on the side makes sense. Another approach: only have ai generate an outline.

comments.author: samcat116
comments.text: Am I correct in assuming it was trying to shut down over an OTA update? I understand the desire for totally owning your device from a software perspective, but would it have just been easier to install the update and then put it back in kiosk mode? Or is there something else I'm missing

comments.author: mdaniel
comments.text:
Heh, well, ironically had it actually applied the OTA then, if I followed the story correctly, they would have forever(?) been locked out of their own device, whereas now they can presumably keep patching root on top of the OTA

Also, in the spirit of "my hardware, my rules," the device should not have been able to shut itself down anyway. It should have advised OP that an update was available for them to install at their convenience

comments.author: derat
comments.text: My impression has been that Amazon sells Fire tablets at or below cost, with the intent of turning a profit through the future sale of media or apps via Amazon's online store. There are methods for bypassing the restrictions and sideloading APKs, Google Play Services, the Play Store, etc., but these are frequently broken by OTA updates. The OP may have been hoping to avoid this by disabling OTA updates.
